131: Good conduct lifts you high. Guard it more carefully than life itself.
132: Guard good conduct with effort. Many virtues help, but this one helps most.
133: Good conduct is true nobility of birth; bad conduct sinks a person low.
134: A learned man who forgets his books can study them again. But one who loses good conduct loses even his high standing.
135: As the envious never have wealth, the one without good conduct never has greatness.
136: The firm-hearted never slacken in right conduct — they know the misery that breaking it brings.
137: Right conduct brings greatness. Wrong conduct brings unbearable disgrace.
138: Right conduct is the seed of virtue. Wrong conduct only ever brings sorrow.
139: Those versed in right conduct will not speak evil even by accident.
140: However much you have studied, if you cannot live well with the world, you are still ignorant.
141: The folly of craving another's wife is not found in those who understand virtue and the rights of others.
142: Among all fools outside virtue's gate, the greatest are those who linger at a neighbour's door.
143: Those who desire evil toward another's wife are no better than dead men.
144: However great he may be, what worth is left if he ignores all guilt and goes to another's wife?
145: Whoever takes lightly the path to another's wife takes on a stain that never fades.
146: Hatred, sin, fear, and disgrace — these four never leave the one who goes to a neighbour's wife.
147: He who does not desire a woman bound to another is praised as a virtuous householder.
148: The noble strength that never looks at another's wife — that is the virtue and dignity of the great.
149: Who thrives in this world, girded by the fearsome sea? Those who never touch another's spouse.
150: Even a person full of faults does one thing right if they never covet another's spouse.
153: To turn away guests is poverty of poverty. To bear with the ignorant is might of might.
154: If you want greatness never to leave you, keep patience alive in your conduct.
156: The angry person's pleasure lasts a day. The patient person's praise lasts till the world's end.
158: Overcome with patience those who commit excesses out of pride.
159: Those who bear the rude speech of the arrogant are as pure as ascetics.
160: Great are those who fast. Greater still are those who bear others' harsh words.
161: Hold a heart free of envy as dear as you hold good conduct itself.
162: Of every excellence a person can gain, none equals being free of envy.
163: Whoever resents another's success instead of rejoicing in it — people will say he wants both virtue and wealth.
164: The wise, knowing the misery wrongdoing brings, will not let envy push them into unjust deeds.
165: Envy needs no enemies. By itself it can bring a person down.
166: Whoever burns at the gifts given to others will come to want, he and his family with him.
167: Fortune turns away from the envious and leads misfortune to them instead.
168: Envy wastes your wealth here, and hereafter it digs you a pit of fire.
169: The world will wonder at the envious man's wealth and the good man's poverty.
170: The envious have never become great. The free of envy have never lacked greatness.
171: The moment someone abandons fairness and covets another's property, his family is ruined and guilt begins.
172: Those who blush at unfairness will not commit shameful acts for the sake of profit.
173: Those who long for higher joys will not trade them for small pleasures here.
174: The wise, even in want, will not covet another's goods.
175: What good is vast, exact knowledge if greed makes a person act senselessly toward everyone?
176: Even the kindly householder, if he starts to covet and scheme, will come to ruin.
177: Do not crave greedy gains. There is no glory in enjoying what greed wins.
178: What is the wealth that never perishes? Freedom from greed.
179: Fortune herself rushes to the wise who, knowing it is virtue, do not covet what belongs to others.
180: Greed without caution destroys. The greatness that wants nothing wins.
181: Even a person lost in vice does one thing right if they never backbite.
182: The worst of all sins: reviling someone behind their back, then smiling to their face.
183: The two-faced backbiter would gain more from death than from life.
184: Even if you cannot speak kindly to a person's face, never say behind their back what will do harm later.
185: One who praises virtue in public but slanders in private shows how empty his heart is.
186: Whoever spreads others' faults — their own faults will be hunted out and spread abroad.
187: Those who cannot live in warm friendship with cheerful talk will drive away even their own kin by backbiting.
188: What would they not do to strangers — people who cannot even keep their dear friends' faults private?
189: The world tolerates even those who revile others only behind their backs.
190: If we watched our own faults as closely as we watch others', would any evil be left in the world?
191: Whoever bores everyone with useless talk will be despised by all.
192: To waste a crowd's time with empty talk is a greater wrong than even hurting your friends.
193: Empty talk will earn its speaker a name: "he has no virtue."
194: Words that neither help nor delight have no place in a good life.
195: Even the good lose their standing if they let vain words slip.
196: Do not call him a person who rattles on emptily. Call him the chaff of humankind.
197: The wise may speak plainly; they never speak pointlessly.
198: The wise who seek the rarest pleasures will not let weightless words leave their lips.
199: The wise, faultless and free of ignorance, will not speak useless words even by forgetfulness.
200: Speak what is useful. Leave useless words unsaid.
201: Ordinary people do not fear doing wrong. The excellent fear even a hint of it.
202: Evil produces evil. That is why it must be feared more than fire.
203: Wisdom's highest law: never do to others what, in their place, you would not want done to you.
204: The one who plots another's ruin — virtue itself plots his ruin in return.
205: Do not commit evil saying "I am poor." Doing it makes you poorer still.
206: Whoever does not want sorrow chasing them must do no evil to others.
207: One can live down any enemy. Sin as an enemy hunts without rest and kills.
208: Ruin dogs the heels of evil-doers like a shadow that never leaves.
209: If you love yourself, do no sin, however small it seems.
210: Know this: whoever does no evil, and never strays from the straight path, is beyond destruction.
211: Kindness asks for no return. What does the world ever pay back to the clouds?
212: Everything the good work hard to earn is meant to be shared.
213: In this world or any other, no good equals the good of giving.
214: One who knows and practices giving truly lives. One who does not is counted among the dead.
215: The wealth of one who loves to give is like a city tank full to its brim.
216: The wealth of the generous is like a fruit tree standing ripe in the middle of a town.
217: Wealth in a generous person's hands is like a village tree that cures every sickness.
218: The wise who know their duty never stint on giving, even when poor.
219: The only poverty of the kind-hearted is not being able to give.
220: If giving costs you, that cost is worth paying even with your own self.
221: Giving to the destitute is true charity. Every other gift expects a return.
222: To beg is wrong, even if it opened heaven. To give is right, even if it shut it.
223: Great people never say "I have nothing." They find a way to give even in hardship.
224: A beggar at the door is hard to look at — until you give, and see his face brighten.
225: The ascetic's power is enduring hunger. Greater is the power of those who end others' hunger.
226: The best treasury for your wealth is the hungry poor you relieve.
227: Hunger's fire never burns the one who gives food to others before eating.
228: Do those who store and lose their wealth not know the happiness giving brings?
229: Eating alone, sharing nothing, just to grow richer — that is the greater wrong.
230: Nothing is harder than death — yet even death is sweeter than wanting to give and finding no way.
231: Give to the poor and live in praise. There is no greater profit for a person.
232: Every fine word spoken in this world settles as praise on the one who gives to the poor.
233: Nothing in this world lasts except fame — it stands alone and does not perish.
234: The one who wins true fame on earth outshines even the sages praised in heaven.
235: Only the wise know how to trade this dying body for a deathless name.
236: If you are born at all, be born for a good name. Better not born than live without one.
237: If you have won no praise, why blame the ones who look down on you? Blame yourself instead.
238: To the wise, leaving no good name behind is itself a disgrace.
239: The very earth yields less to one who lives without a good name.
240: A life without disgrace is life. A life without honor is no life at all.
241: Kindness is the truest wealth. Money alone even the worst of people can have.
242: Whatever your creed, think it through and be kind. Kindness is the best guide of all.
243: Those whose hearts are the home of kindness will never enter the world of darkness.
244: The wise say no dreaded evil befalls the one who is kind and guards the lives of other creatures.
245: This broad earth, over which the wind blows, bears witness: sorrow never touches the kind-hearted.
246: Those who give up kindness for cruelty, the wise say, forgot their past lessons and the sorrow ahead.
247: As this world is not for those without wealth, the next world is not for those without kindness.
248: The poor may grow rich one day. Those without kindness are poor beyond repair.
249: The goodness of the unkind is as empty as a blind man's sight of God.
250: Before you crush the weak, remember how you once trembled before the strong.
251: How can he have kindness who eats the flesh of other creatures to fatten his own flesh?
252: As none can call careless wealth their own, none can call a flesh-eater kind.
253: Like the mind of one who carries a weapon, the mind that feasts with pleasure on another creature's body has no room for goodness.
254: If you ask what kindness is and what its opposite — saving life and taking it. So eating flesh cannot be right.
255: Sparing flesh keeps life whole. The flesh-eater, once fallen into hell, will find no way back out.
256: If the world stopped killing for food, who would sell flesh for coin?
257: If people truly knew that flesh is the unclean sore of a body, they would stop eating it.
258: The wise, free of delusion, do not eat what was cut from another's body.
259: To spare a life is worth more than a thousand offerings of ghee.
260: Every living creature bows in worship to the one who has never taken life nor tasted flesh.
